prize_parts.citation: For turning the ubiquitin-proteasome system into a chemical tool: induced-proximity degraders and the cereblon mechanism of molecular glues

statement.case_for: Targeted protein degradation converts a biological process, ubiquitin-dependent proteolysis, into a designable chemical reaction at the protein surface. Heterobifunctional PROTACs (Crews, Deshaies) and monovalent molecular glues, whose mechanism became chemically explicable once Handa identified cereblon as the thalidomide target, share one principle: a small molecule induces a ternary complex and catalytic, event-driven removal of the target. The principle is general, has been reproduced by many independent academic and industrial groups, and the ternary-complex and ubiquitin-transfer steps are being measured quantitatively. It reaches proteins once considered undruggable and has produced approved glue-class drugs and late-stage degrader trials. Five of eight members ranked it, four in their top three, which is the broadest support on the shortlist, and my own field (nucleotide metabolism, where RNR and dNTP-pool enzymes are classic hard targets) gives me practical reason to value the capability.
statement.case_against: No heterobifunctional PROTAC is yet an approved drug, so the clinical case rests on glue-class medicines and on trial data. Credit is also genuinely split: PROTAC concept (Crews, Deshaies, Sakamoto), structure-guided ligand and ternary-complex work (Ciulli), and the cereblon/glue strand (Handa, Ito, Gray) are related but distinct, and any three names exclude people with real claims, notably Sakamoto, Ciulli and Gray. A citation that bundles the two strands may be criticised as stitching, while a PROTAC-only prize leaves the best-validated medicines unexplained.

responses.point: Heiner ranks B010 third with Crews, Deshaies and Ciulli, and asks whether PROTACs and molecular glues should be combined or separated in the citation, noting that approval of a PROTAC is still pending.
responses.response: I take the question about separating the strands seriously, but I would keep one part. Both act through the same chemical logic of induced proximity to an E3 ligase, and the cereblon finding is what shows that the thalidomide class, already in patients, works by this mechanism. That is why I prefer Handa to Ciulli in the third slot: Ciulli's VHL ligand and ternary-complex work is excellent, but it refines the PROTAC strand, whereas Handa supplies the mechanism that explains the glue strand and the existing drugs. I accept that this leaves Ciulli out and would reconsider if the committee wants a PROTAC-only citation; on the approval point I think the medicines already in use through cereblon give clinical maturity that a PROTAC-only reading would lack.

responses.point: Johan puts massively parallel sequencing (B011) first as the clearest game-changer, a chemical solution of reversible terminators and clustered surfaces that is overdue, and places B010 second with timing somewhat early because clinical validation is incomplete.
responses.response: I agree that B011 is mature and that the impact is exceptional, and it is my own third choice. My reservation is not about merit but about the allocation. The credited list mixes the Solexa chemistry (Balasubramanian, Klenerman), the competing 454 platform (Rothberg) and the contested contributions of Ju and Mayer, and any three-person split needs a choice between platform lineages that I cannot verify from the supplied material. For B010 the principle and its mechanism are more cleanly connected to named people. On Johan's point about early timing for degraders, I would weigh the quantitative mechanistic evidence and glue-class medicines more than the absence of an approved PROTAC. I also do not see B028 as an independent route to a sequencing prize, since it overlaps with B011.

responses.point: Emma ranks the phase-separation candidate (B046) first and proposes three UBC-centred names for the lipid nanoparticle candidate (B051), arguing that the physical-chemical design principles are chemical and mature, while also noting that B046 is somewhat early.
responses.response: On B051 I agree with Emma that the pH-dependent ionizable-lipid design is real chemistry and clinically validated at scale, but I would rank it below B010 because the credit is diffuse between academic and company inventors, and because the formulation character could sit better with Medicine. Her three-name UBC trio (Cullis, Hope, Madden) differs from my own selection that included Anderson and MacLachlan, which shows how unsettled the allocation is. On B046 I share her view that the concept is valuable, but the open question of which condensates are truly equilibrium phase-separated, and a measurement-level uncertainty about in-cell function, makes me more cautious than she is about timing.

responses.point: Peter ranks long-range electron transfer in proteins (B043) first and nitrogenase (B058) second, valuing mechanism-first biophysical chemistry with decades of independent confirmation.
responses.response: I share Peter's preference for mechanism over phenomenology and rank nitrogenase fifth for exactly that reason, but I think B058 is held back by the unsettled catalytic mechanism: the structures are secure, yet N2 binding and the reduction cycle are still debated, and any three-person set omits Dean, Ribbe and other spectroscopists. For B043 I find the science convincing but the supplied material gives me no basis to place it above degraders, as it is already textbook knowledge and a prize for it would be recognition of a long-settled result rather than of a capability that is changing practice.

uncertainties: Whether the committee prefers a combined PROTAC-and-glue citation or a narrower one, and whether Handa or Ciulli is the better third name.
Whether the lack of an approved heterobifunctional degrader makes the timing premature for colleagues who weight clinical outcomes.
Priority details are recalled from the literature and have not been independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from the provided profile. My work on dNTP pools and ribonucleotide reductase is not directly tied to any shortlisted candidate, and I have no recorded collaboration with the credited names.
